lead: An open section, such as a channel, Z, angle or lipped stringer, has free edges where the shear flow must be zero. Starting there and integrating along the wall gives the whole shear flow distribution; taking moments of it gives the shear centre. Below, the general integral is worked on a Z-section with I<sub>xy</sub> ≠ 0 and on a channel stiffened by booms.
prereq: You need: shear flow and the shear centre from the first chapter, and Ixx, Iyy and Ixy of thin-walled sections from the topic on bending.

sections.h3: From a free edge to a shear flow

blocks.text: Cut a piece of wall between a free edge and a point at distance s along the wall mid-line. On the two faces of a slice dz long the direct stress differs by (∂σ/∂z) dz. The only force that can balance that difference is the shear flow on the cut, so ∂q/∂s = −t ∂σ/∂z. Using the unsymmetrical bending stress and dM<sub>x</sub>/dz = S<sub>y</sub>, dM<sub>y</sub>/dz = S<sub>x</sub>, and integrating from q = 0 at the free edge:

q<sub>s</sub> = −[(S<sub>x</sub> I<sub>xx</sub> − S<sub>y</sub> I<sub>xy</sub>)/D] ∫₀ˢ t x ds − [(S<sub>y</sub> I<sub>yy</sub> − S<sub>x</sub> I<sub>xy</sub>)/D] ∫₀ˢ t y ds,   D = I<sub>xx</sub> I<sub>yy</sub> − I<sub>xy</sub>²
blocks.where: q<sub>s</sub> is the shear flow at s (N/mm), positive in the direction of increasing s; S<sub>x</sub> and S<sub>y</sub> are the shear force components (N); x and y are centroidal coordinates of the wall element (mm); I<sub>xx</sub>, I<sub>yy</sub> and I<sub>xy</sub> are centroidal second moments (mm⁴); D is in mm⁸.

blocks.text: If the section is symmetric about x (I<sub>xy</sub> = 0) and S<sub>x</sub> = 0, this reduces to q<sub>s</sub> = −(S<sub>y</sub>/I<sub>xx</sub>) ∫ t y ds. The equation assumes the shear acts through the shear centre, so the section does not twist. Choosing the other free edge as the start reverses every sign but not the physical flow.

sections.h3: Working round a section, and finding the shear centre

items: Find the centroid and I<sub>xx</sub>, I<sub>yy</sub> and I<sub>xy</sub> using mid-line dimensions.
Pick a free edge, the direction of s, and write x and y of each wall as functions of s.
Integrate wall by wall. Carry the value at the end of one wall into the start of the next: q is continuous round a corner.
Check that q returns to zero at the other free edge, and that the vertical walls add up to S<sub>y</sub>.
Take moments of all the q ds about a convenient point O and set them equal to the moment of the load placed at the unknown shear centre.

blocks.text: In a channel the two flange flows form a couple, which pushes the shear centre out beyond the web. A Z-section with equal flanges has point symmetry, so its shear centre is at the centroid. With I<sub>xy</sub> ≠ 0 the x term in the formula is not zero, and q can change sign along a flange: a zero inside a wall is not a free edge.

A real stringer or spar has concentrated areas: spar caps, lips, attached stringers. Idealise each as a boom of area B<sub>r</sub> at (x<sub>r</sub>, y<sub>r</sub>) that carries all the direct stress, and let the thin walls between booms carry only shear. Walls of this kind are said to be ineffective in bending. The integral then contributes nothing between booms, so q is constant along each wall and jumps at each boom:

q₂ − q₁ = −[(S<sub>x</sub> I<sub>xx</sub> − S<sub>y</sub> I<sub>xy</sub>)/D] B<sub>r</sub> x<sub>r</sub> − [(S<sub>y</sub> I<sub>yy</sub> − S<sub>x</sub> I<sub>xy</sub>)/D] B<sub>r</sub> y<sub>r</sub>
blocks.where: q₁ and q₂ are the flows just before and just after boom r along the direction of s (N/mm); B<sub>r</sub> is the boom area (mm²); x<sub>r</sub> and y<sub>r</sub> its centroidal coordinates (mm). With I<sub>xy</sub> = 0 and S<sub>x</sub> = 0 it is q₂ − q₁ = −(S<sub>y</sub>/I<sub>xx</sub>) B<sub>r</sub> y<sub>r</sub>.

blocks.text: If the walls also carry direct stress, keep both: the integral for each wall plus the jump at each boom. The structural idealisation chapter shows how to choose B for a stringer and its skin.

figure.caption: The worked Z-section's shear flow, unrolled along its wall from the top flange tip. Because I<sub>xy</sub> ≠ 0 the flow changes sign inside each flange (up to +5.02 N/mm, then −16.07 N/mm at the corners); it peaks at −48.21 N/mm where the web crosses the neutral axis and returns to zero at the bottom tip.

spec.aria: Left: a Z-section with its top flange to the right and bottom flange to the left, the centroid G marked as the shear centre. Right: a graph of shear flow against distance along the wall from the top tip, 0 to 160 millimetres. The curve starts at zero, rises to about plus 5 in the top flange, falls to minus 16.07 at the corner at 40 millimetres, reaches minus 48.21 at mid-web at 80 millimetres, climbs back to minus 16.07 at the lower corner at 120, rises to about plus 5 and ends at zero at 160.

examples.question: A Z-section has a web 80 mm deep and two flanges 40 mm wide, all 2 mm thick; the top flange runs from the web to x = +40 mm, the bottom flange to x = −40 mm. It carries S<sub>y</sub> = 3 kN (S<sub>x</sub> = 0) through its shear centre. Find the shear flow at 10 mm steps from the top free edge, and the shear centre.
steps: Origin at the centroid (web mid-height). I<sub>xx</sub> = 2 × 80³/12 + 2 × 80 × 40² = 341,333 mm⁴. I<sub>yy</sub> = 2 × (2 × 40³/3) = 85,333 mm⁴. I<sub>xy</sub> = 2 × 80 × 20 × 40 = 128,000 mm⁴ (flanges in the first and third quadrants). D = 1.274 × 10¹⁰ mm⁸.
With S<sub>x</sub> = 0: q = (S<sub>y</sub> I<sub>xy</sub>/D) ∫t x ds − (S<sub>y</sub> I<sub>yy</sub>/D) ∫t y ds = 0.030134 ∫t x ds − 0.020089 ∫t y ds (N/mm³).

Bottom flange, s from the web: x = −s, y = −40. q = −16.071 − 0.030134s² + 0.020089(80s). At s = 10 … 40: −3.013, 4.018, 5.022, 0.000 N/mm. It returns to zero at the free tip, which checks the arithmetic.

Resultants: the top flange gives ∫q ds = 0.030134 × 42,667 − 0.020089 × 64,000 = 0, and so does the bottom flange. The web gives ∫q ds = −3,000 N along +s (downwards), that is 3000 N upwards = S<sub>y</sub>.
Shear centre: the flanges carry no net force and the web lies on x = 0, so the moment of the flows about the centroid is zero. The shear centre is at the centroid, as point symmetry requires.
examples.answer: q runs 0, 5.02, 4.02, −3.01, −16.07 along the top flange, down to −48.214 N/mm at mid-web, and back to zero at the bottom tip; the shear centre is at the centroid.

examples.question: A channel spar is idealised as four booms on a 200 mm deep web: 200 mm² at each flange tip (x = 80 mm) and 400 mm² at each web corner (x = 0), at y = ±100 mm. The walls carry shear only. It carries S<sub>y</sub> = 12 kN through its shear centre. Find the shear flows and the shear centre.
steps: I<sub>xx</sub> = Σ B y² = 2 × (200 + 400) × 100² = 12,000,000 mm⁴, and S<sub>y</sub>/I<sub>xx</sub> = 0.0010 N/mm³.
Top flange, from the free tip boom 1: q₁₂ = −0.0010 × 200 × 100 = −20.0 N/mm (s runs from the tip to the corner).
Web, after corner boom 2: q₂₃ = −20.0 − 0.0010 × 400 × 100 = −60.0 N/mm.
Bottom flange, after corner boom 3 (y = −100): q₃₄ = −60.0 + 0.0010 × 400 × 100 = −20.0 N/mm. After tip boom 4: −20.0 + 20.0 = 0, the free edge. Check.
Web force: 60 N/mm × 200 mm = 12,000 N = S<sub>y</sub>. Each flange carries 20 × 80 = 1,600 N, in opposite directions: a couple of 1,600 × 200 = 320,000 N·mm.
Moments about the web: S<sub>y</sub> e = 320,000, so e = 26.67 mm from the web, on the side away from the flanges.
examples.answer: 20 N/mm in each flange, 60 N/mm in the web, zero beyond the tip booms; the shear centre is 26.67 mm outside the web.

traps: Setting q = 0 at a web–flange corner. Only the free tips of an open section have q = 0.
Dropping I<sub>xy</sub> on a Z or angle. Then the x term vanishes and the flange flows come out with the wrong shape.
Using |y| instead of the signed coordinate. Below the neutral axis y is negative and the integral starts to fall.

quiz.q: Write the shear flow in an open section symmetric about x under S<sub>y</sub> alone, and define each symbol.
quiz.a: q<sub>s</sub> = −(S<sub>y</sub>/I<sub>xx</sub>) ∫₀ˢ t y ds: S<sub>y</sub> shear force (N), I<sub>xx</sub> second moment about the centroidal x axis (mm⁴), t thickness (mm), y signed coordinate (mm), s distance from the free edge (mm).

quiz.q: Why is q not zero at a web–flange corner, even though the flange started at zero?
quiz.a: At the corner the flange delivers its flow into the web. Equilibrium of a small corner element needs the web flow to start at the flange value, so q is continuous round the corner.

quiz.q: In the Z-section example, find q 20 mm down the web.
Why is the shear centre of an equal-flange Z at its centroid, while a channel's is outside the web?
quiz.a: The Z has point symmetry about the centroid: each flange carries zero net force and the web passes through the centroid, so the flows have no moment about it. In the channel both flanges carry equal and opposite forces that form a couple, so the vertical resultant must sit off the web to balance it.

quiz.q: In the stiffened channel, what happens to the shear centre if the tip booms are removed?
quiz.a: With no tip booms the flanges carry no flow (q₁₂ = 0), the couple vanishes, and the shear centre moves onto the web line. Stiffening the tips increases the flange flows and moves the shear centre outwards.

beyond: Not for the exam. The shear centre of an open stringer decides whether it buckles in pure bending or in combined bending and twist. Search for "flexural–torsional buckling of stringers".
